searches.note: Twenty four searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's, four left unspent. The three shared searches went to the orders that drew and renamed the sub-region (Portaria 28/2001 on the open web, then Portaria 291/2009 restricted to the Diário da República, the IVV and the CVRVV) and to the Monção co-operative's first bottling, for the plan's why and the region's line on the Brejoeira. The houses' own domains were searched by restriction three times (soalheiro.com, the Aveleda and Casal Garcia domains twice), each read as primary through its summary; the rest went to the open web with the author's sources blocked (the houses' domains, Palm Bay, Skurnik, VinoVoss, Portugal Vineyards, the Portuguese Wikipedia, the DGPC, Esporão, Wine Industry Advisor, Harpers) so that an independent account could be heard. No fetch tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the orders and their years, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the governing texts (the Diário da República's orders of 2001 and 2009, the CVRVV's press kit), then to independent accounts of each house's dates and people, then to merchants' sheets of each wine for the blend, the months and the vessels, with the author's sources blocked.

Where a fact rested on the Codex alone (Soalheiro's added carbon dioxide) or on no source the refuter could find (the royal household, the slowing by the plan, the visitors since 2010, the estate given over to one grape), it was taken out; where accounts disagree and the record tells the house's version, the tension is named (the Brejoeira's companion) or left open.

tested: The founding, the open web with the house's domain and Palm Bay blocked: Thorman Hunt and Decanter's vertical give the founder planting Melgaço's first continuous Alvarinho vineyard in 1974 on a family plot named Soalheiro for its sun, and the brand launched in 1982; Decanter calls him the local tax collector and a self taught grower, and Monção e Melgaço's fourth producer with that launch. Borne out: the 1974 vineyard, the 1982 brand, the finance office, the name of the plot. The garage is on the house's page and Different Drop only, told as the house's account.

The making and the service, the house and Palm Bay blocked: Holy Wines gives the must clarified at a low temperature between pressing and fermentation, fermentation in stainless steel and maturing on fine lees before bottling; Different Drop gives steel at a low temperature, fine lees, no oak, no skin contact and no malolactic. Rasch Vin gives 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, Holy Wines 8. Borne out, save the carbon dioxide.

The carbon dioxide, twice: once on soalheiro.com (the Granit, 9%, Revirado and other pages, which say nothing of added gas) and once on the open web (Vivino, Wine Spectator's still white for Primeiras Vinhas, Vinum Lector's dry white). No source read says whether the Classic is given carbon dioxide or not; the claim rested on the library's style line alone and is taken out.

Granit, on the house's page: small vineyards on granite at around 400 metres in Monção e Melgaço, fermented in stainless steel at 22 degrees Celsius, warmer than usual; the house's 2022 harvest page calls the 2015 Granit its first bet on altitude. Borne out.
Primeiras Vinhas: Different Drop and Garrafeira Nacional give it from the original plot of 1974. Borne out.

The label: K&L Wines notes that the front label names Monção e Melgaço rather than Vinho Verde, and the house's Granit page gives Monção and Melgaço, Vinho Verde DOC; the label term was changed to the sub-region the bottle shows.

The house rules: nobody living named (the founder, his wife and their children are described; the founder's name met in Thorman Hunt and Decanter is not used), no price, no score (Decanter's medals and Wine Spectator's listing are not used), nothing volatile, British, no dash.

changed.was: In 1974 a Melgaço family planted a vineyard of Alvarinho near the town, by its own account the first continuous vineyard of the grape in the municipality. The founder, who worked in the local finance office while his wife taught at the primary school, planted it with his parents, and following the local custom of naming land the plot was called Soalheiro, a place that takes the sun. In 1982, again by the house's account, he made and bottled the first wine in the family garage, and Soalheiro became the first Alvarinho brand of Melgaço. The vineyard of 1974 gives the house its Primeiras Vinhas. The next generation of the family, an oenologist among them, later joined the house, which also draws on a circle of local growing families beside its own vines. The range widened to wines such as Granit, from high granite plots, while the plain Soalheiro Alvarinho, made in steel and kept on its fine lees, remained its core. For a sommelier it is the plain lesson in what Melgaço gives Alvarinho: ripeness, weight and length from a sheltered valley, without the prickle of a light Vinho Verde.

tested: The palace, the house's domain, both Wikipedias' Portuguese page and the DGPC blocked: the DGLAB's archive of Viana do Castelo gives the building begun about 1806 by Luís Pereira Velho de Moscoso, finished about 1834, and the national monument by the decree of 16 June 1910, published on 23 June; the English Wikipedia gives 1805, National Geographic Portugal the last decade of the eighteenth century and a plan of four façades round a closed court with four towers that was never finished. Borne out: around the turn of the century, about 1834, the decree. Not borne out: a nobleman of the royal household (one account says he was not of the high nobility and asked leave of the Prince Regent for a third tower) and the slowing by the plan's scale.
The plan and the towers: SIPA's record and Portugal by Wine give an L shaped plan, granite and three towers, neoclassical with baroque touches. Borne out.

The family: Executiva, Portugal by Wine, Observador and the Diário de Notícias give the purchase in 1937 by the father, a comendador, as a gift for his daughter, her birth on 21 January 1918, the first Alvarinho in 1964, the cellar of 1974, the launch of 1976 and her death on 30 December 2015 in the private part of the palace. Borne out.

The companion, the house's domain and the Portuguese Wikipedia blocked: Geneall's forum and the Porto de Antanho blog tell of an auction after the father's bankruptcy, the estate bought by her companion, who planted the Alvarinho and built the cellar; one source gives 1977 for the launch. The record now says other accounts give much of that work to him; he is not named, for want of dates.

The making and the service, the house and Portugal Vineyards blocked: Mistral gives fermentation in temperature controlled stainless steel, no oak barrel, six months in the cellars before release and 9 to 12 degrees Celsius; Wine & Stuff whole bunch pressing and steel throughout; Bin Ends steel and lees; Santa Luzia six to eight months in bottle and 8 to 10 degrees Celsius. Borne out, and steel and no oak now stand on two sheets.

The house rules: the woman is named with her dates, which three sources give; the builder, his son, her father, the agronomist of 1964 and the companion are described, not named, for want of dates; the sale of the estate in 2025 (Público) is left out as recent; the visitors since 2010 cut as unsourced and volatile; British, no dash.

changed.was: The Palácio da Brejoeira stands at Pinheiros, just south of Monção: an L shaped palace of granite with three towers, built in the neoclassical style for a nobleman of the royal household. Work began around the turn of the nineteenth century and was finished only about 1834, slowed in part by the sheer scale of the plan. A decree of 16 June 1910 classed it a national monument. In 1937 the palace changed hands again, bought by a father as a gift for his daughter, Maria Hermínia d'Oliveira Paes (1918 to 2015). By the house's account she restructured the estate and in 1964 began planting its first Alvarinho; in 1974 she had a cellar built, and in 1976 the Palácio da Brejoeira Alvarinho was launched, bottled at the estate. She lived in the private part of the palace until her death on 30 December 2015. Since 2010 the palace and its gardens have been open to visitors, and the estate also distils its Alvarinho into an old brandy aged in French oak. For a sommelier, Brejoeira is the estate Alvarinho of Monção: one grape and one estate, with a palace on the label and bottlings that go back to 1976.
changed.now: The Palácio da Brejoeira stands at Pinheiros, just south of Monção: an L shaped palace of granite with three towers, built in the neoclassical style for the owner of the Brejoeira estate. Work began around the turn of the nineteenth century and was finished only about 1834. A decree of 16 June 1910 classed it a national monument. In 1937 the palace changed hands again, bought by a father as a gift for his daughter, Maria Hermínia d'Oliveira Paes (1918 to 2015). By the house's account she restructured the estate and in 1964 began planting its first Alvarinho; in 1974 she had a cellar built, and in 1976 the Palácio da Brejoeira Alvarinho was launched, bottled at the estate; other accounts give much of that work to her companion. She lived in the private part of the palace until her death on 30 December 2015. The estate also distils its Alvarinho into an old brandy aged in French oak. For a sommelier, Brejoeira is the estate Alvarinho of Monção: one grape and one estate, with a palace on the label and bottlings that go back to 1976.
changed.why: The builder is undated in the sources read and one account says he was not of the high nobility, so he is the owner of the estate; the slowing by the plan's scale is in no source read; the opening to visitors since 2010 was found in no source read and is volatile after the sale of 2025; the companion's part is told as other accounts.

tested: The renaming of the sub-region, two shared searches, the second restricted to the Diário da República, the IVV and the CVRVV: Portaria 28/2001 of 16 January 2001 (the Diário da República and FAOLEX) recognised the sub-regions of Vinho Verde, among them Monção, made up of the municipalities of Monção and Melgaço, and reserved Vinho Verde Alvarinho to it; Portaria 291/2009 of 23 March 2009 renamed that sub-region Monção e Melgaço and had every Monção of the 2001 order read as Monção e Melgaço; Portaria 668/2010 cites the 2001 order as amended in 2009, and the CVRVV's press kit says the sub-region was first Monção and later Monção e Melgaço. Not borne out: a decree law of 16 January 2001 that renamed it.

The founding, the house's domain and Skurnik blocked: Winekeller, Blend All About Wine and others give the first Muros de Melgaço Alvarinho of 1998 from a small property in Penso, between Monção and Melgaço, the project begun in 1997 by some accounts; Quinta dos Muros by that name was found in none. Borne out: 1998 and Penso; the quinta's name stays the house's account.

The founder, the same blocks: Jornal de Vinhos and Enoteca give his birth in Monção in a family that had lived from farming and wine for generations, a degree in agro-industrial engineering and a post-graduate course in oenology, and work as an oenologist from 1988. The story's family that made wine for its own table and its agronomy were changed.

Muros Antigos's making, the same blocks: the house's sheet hosted elsewhere, Center Gourmet and Nelsons give destemming, cold settling of 48 to 72 hours, a long fermentation at 14 to 18 degrees Celsius in stainless steel, and at least three months on fine lees with regular stirring, four in other vintages. Borne out.

Parcela Única, the same blocks: Vinha Alvarinho, Estado Líquido and Bodeboca give fermentation in new 400 litre French oak barrels and nine months in them with stirring on the lees, one retailer used barrels in one line. Borne out.
Muros Antigos Escolha: the house's page and Aged Cork give Alvarinho of Monção e Melgaço, Loureiro of the Lima and Avesso of Baião. Borne out.

The house rules: the founder is living and is never named in prose (the house keeps its name); no price (a title met with a price in it is not cited), no score, nothing volatile (the hectares met in two results are not used), British, no dash.

changed.was: The house of Anselmo Mendes carries the name of its founder, an oenologist born in Monção to a farming family that made wine for its own table. He studied agronomy, specialised in wine and worked as an oenologist on several projects before setting out on his own. In 1998, by the house's account, he launched wines under his own signature in Monção e Melgaço and made his first Alvarinhos in a small cellar at Quinta dos Muros in Penso, Melgaço; the walled quinta gave its name to the Muros de Melgaço and Muros Antigos ranges. Three years later a decree law of 16 January 2001 renamed the sub-region, until then named for Monção alone, as Monção e Melgaço. The house became known for testing what Alvarinho can take: long ageing on the lees, fermentation and ageing in new oak barrels for Parcela Única, and Curtimenta, made with time on the skins. Muros Antigos stayed the unoaked core of the range, joined by Escolha, a blend of Alvarinho, Loureiro and Avesso. For a sommelier it is the measure of the house without wood: Alvarinho kept fresh and dry, and given texture by its lees rather than by oak.
changed.now: The house of Anselmo Mendes carries the name of its founder, an oenologist born in Monção to a farming family with vines of its own. He studied agro-industrial engineering and then oenology, and worked as an oenologist for other houses before setting out on his own. In 1998, by the house's account, he launched wines under his own signature in Monção e Melgaço and made his first Alvarinhos in a small cellar at Quinta dos Muros in Penso, Melgaço; the walled quinta gave its name to the Muros de Melgaço and Muros Antigos ranges. An order of 16 January 2001 drew the sub-regions of Vinho Verde, among them one named Monção that took in Melgaço too, and an order of 23 March 2009 renamed it Monção e Melgaço. The house became known for testing what Alvarinho can take: long ageing on the lees, fermentation and ageing in new oak barrels for Parcela Única, and Curtimenta, made with time on the skins. Muros Antigos stayed the unoaked core of the range, joined by Escolha, a blend of Alvarinho, Loureiro and Avesso. For a sommelier it is the measure of the house without wood: Alvarinho kept fresh and dry, and given texture by its lees rather than by oak.
changed.why: The order of 16 January 2001 is a portaria that drew the sub-regions and named this one Monção; the renaming to Monção e Melgaço is the order of 23 March 2009. The founder's family and his studies follow Jornal de Vinhos and Enoteca.

changed.was: Quinta do Ameal lies along the bank of the Lima at Refóios do Lima, by Ponte de Lima, and its records go back to 1710. In the 1990s the estate passed to a family that set out to show what Loureiro, the Lima valley's own white grape, could do on its own, and by the house's own account Ameal became a pioneer in showing that the grape could make white wine of real quality on its own. In 2000 the estate made its first trials of Loureiro aged in French oak barrels, the beginning of the wine first called Escolha and later Reserva, which comes from its Marinhas plot. In 2019 the estate was sold to Esporão, the Alentejo house, which kept its work on Loureiro and bottles its wines under the name Ameal. The flagship stayed what it had been: Loureiro alone from the estate, fermented in steel and kept on its fine lees for months. For a sommelier, Ameal Loureiro is the lesson in the Lima's grape, made with the care Monção e Melgaço gives Alvarinho, and the proof that a serious Vinho Verde can rest on a single grape other than Alvarinho.
